newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Shevardnadze, separatists held talks - spokesman.
newsitem.headline: Shevardnadze, separatists held talks - spokesman.

text.p: Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze and top officials from the separatist region of Abkhazia held secret talks last week, the presidential press service said on Monday.

Press Secretary Vakho Abashidze said Shevardnadze met Abkhaz "foreign minister" Konstantin Ozgan in the capital Tbilisi last Thursday. Daur Barganzhiya, a member of the self-styled Abkhaz parliament, also attended, he said.

The visit is the first to Georgia proper by a high-ranking Abkhaz official since the end of full-scale war between the two sides in 1993. Previous talks mediated by the United Nations and Russia have taken place in Europe or Moscow.
Abashidze declined to say if any concrete progress was made during the negotiations.

"They discussed the full range of questions regarding the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict," he said, adding that the two men also talked about a possible meeting between separatist Abkhaz leader Vladislav Ardzinba and Shevardnadze.

Georgia and the U.N. have condemned the Abkhaz plans to hold a parliamentary vote on Saturday, saying that tens of thousands of refugees must first be allowed to return to the subtropical Black Sea region and its political status resolved.
Ethnic Georgians once accounted for 45 percent of the region's population but the majority of them fled after the Abkhaz takeover, fearing ethnic cleansing.
Shevardnadze on Monday repeated his opposition to the poll, calling it a "masquerade". "Georgia has a firm position on these illegal elections," he said in his weekly radio address.
Georgia sent troops to the resort region in 1992 to try to quell demands by the local parliament for more autonomy.
The Abkhaz, helped by the Russian military, swept to victory after a year of fighting that killed 10,000 people and they have run their own affairs ever since.
Neogotiations are deadlocked with Tbilisi offering only autonomy while the Abkhaz want either total or virtual independence.
The self-declared state has been shunned by the international community and a partial blockade by the Commonwealth of Independent States has crippled its economy.
